name: How Many Hospitals Use AI
blurb: Survey data on AI adoption in US hospitals.
title: How Many Hospitals Use AI
answer: Hospital AI use is growing but not yet universal. A national study published in December 2025 found about a third of US hospitals were current AI users and a quarter more planned to adopt within a year. FDA device authorization counts measure what is allowed on the market, not what hospitals actually use.

reading.body:
About a third of US hospitals used AI as of December 2025, and roughly a quarter more planned to adopt within a year.

The pattern is a market in the middle of a build-out, not one that has finished. A 31.5 percent current-user share with 24.7 percent intending to adopt within twelve months means the installed base could roughly double on stated intent alone. Intent is not deployment, and the gap between the two is where most adoption forecasts go wrong.

For AI specifically, the distinction between authorization and use matters more than in most sectors. FDA device authorization counts measure what is permitted to be sold, not what is running in a hospital. A rising authorization count can coexist with flat clinical use, and the two are routinely conflated.

The data does not say which AI functions hospitals have adopted, how deeply any of them are integrated into clinical workflow, or what happened after the twelve-month window closed. It also does not cover spending, staffing, or the compute and power footprint of hospital AI, so it cannot support claims about infrastructure demand. The one structural finding it does carry is that adoption is far higher in large systems than in small and rural hospitals, which makes any single national percentage a poor guide to what a given care team actually faces.

The 31.5 percent figure is a stock, and the 24.7 percent is a flow. A stock tells you how many hospitals have crossed the line. A flow tells you how many are trying to. When the flow is nearly as large as the stock, the composition of the user base a year later depends almost entirely on whether the intenders convert, and the data gives no conversion rate.

The size and rural split is the more useful cut. A national percentage averages over a distribution that is not flat, so a large system and a critical access hospital can both sit inside "about a third" while facing completely different realities. The practical consequence is that a care team benchmarking itself against the national number learns almost nothing. It should benchmark against hospitals of its own size and type.

Authorization and use are separate ledgers. FDA device authorization counts what may be sold. The survey counts what hospitals report using. Nothing in the data links the two, so a rising authorization count is not evidence of rising clinical use, and a flat authorization count is not evidence of stagnation.

How many US hospitals were using AI as of December 2025?
31.5 percent, according to a JAMA Network Open study published that month. That is about a third of US hospitals.

How many more hospitals planned to adopt AI within a year?
24.7 percent planned adoption within a year. If every one of them followed through, the user base would roughly double.

Does the data show whether those hospitals actually adopted?
No. The data records stated intent as of December 2025 and does not report what happened after the twelve-month window.

Is hospital AI adoption higher in some hospitals than others?
Yes. Adoption is far higher in large systems than in small and rural hospitals. The data does not give separate percentages for each group.

Does a rising FDA device authorization count mean more hospitals are using AI?
No. Authorization counts measure what is allowed on the market, not what hospitals use. The data does not connect the two measures.

Which AI functions have hospitals adopted, and how deeply are they integrated?
The data does not say. It reports adoption as a single yes-or-no status and carries no breakdown by function or by depth of clinical integration.
